milestones.title: Milestone 1: Introduction to React and JSX

lessons.title: Lesson 1: React Intro

sections.heading: What is React?
sections.content: React is a front-end JavaScript library developed by Facebook Software Engineer Jordan Walke. Also known as React.js or ReactJS, it is a tool for building UI components.

sections.heading: How does React Work?
sections.content: React creates a Virtual DOM in memory. Instead of manipulating the browser's DOM directly, React performs all manipulations in the virtual DOM first, then applies only the necessary changes to the real browser DOM. React finds out what changes have been made and changes only what needs to be changed.

sections.heading: Prerequisites
sections.content: Before learning React you should have a basic understanding of HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. The HTML-like code in React uses JSX, which allows writing HTML tags inside JavaScript code.

sections.heading: React Environment
sections.content: To use React in production, you need npm (included with Node.js) and a build tool. In this course, code is written directly via the FrontEndly live server during exercise sections.

sections.heading: Modify the React App
sections.content: Inside a project folder (e.g. my-react-app), the src folder contains App.jsx — the main React component you modify to update the application.

keyTakeaways: React is a JS library for building UI via reusable components.
React uses a Virtual DOM to optimize real DOM updates.
App.jsx in the src folder is the main component to edit.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Rendering HTML in React

sections.heading: The Container
sections.content:
React renders HTML into a web page via a container, typically a
element inside index.html.

sections.heading: The createRoot Function
sections.content: createRoot() is a built-in function (from react-dom/client) used to create a root node for a React application. It takes one argument: an HTML element where a React component should be displayed.
sections.code:
import { StrictMode } from 'react'
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client'
import './index.css'
import App from './App.jsx'

createRoot(document.getElementById('root')).render(
  <StrictMode>
    <App />
  </StrictMode>
)

sections.heading: The render Method
sections.content: The render method defines what to render inside the HTML container. The result is displayed in the <div id="root"> element.
sections.code:
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client' createRoot(document.getElementById('root')).render(

Welcome!

)

sections.heading: The Root Node
sections.content: The root node is the HTML element where you want React to display the result. It does NOT have to be a <div>, and it does NOT have to have id='root' — it can be named anything.

keyTakeaways: createRoot(element).render(jsx) is how React mounts an app.
The root node element can have any id/tag name, not just <div id='root'>.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Introduction to JSX

sections.heading: What is JSX?
sections.content: JSX stands for JavaScript XML. It allows writing HTML in React and makes it easier to write and add HTML inside React code.

sections.heading: Coding JSX
sections.content: JSX lets you write HTML elements in JavaScript and place them in the DOM without createElement() or appendChild(). JSX converts HTML tags into React elements. Using JSX is optional but recommended.

sections.heading: Expressions in JSX
sections.content: You can write any valid JavaScript expression inside curly braces { }. JSX executes the expression and returns the result.
sections.code:
const myElement =

React is {5 + 5} times better with JSX

; // Output: React is 10 times better with JSX

sections.heading: Elements Must be Closed
sections.content: JSX follows XML rules — HTML elements must be properly closed (e.g. , ), or JSX throws an error.

sections.heading: Attribute class = className
sections.content: class is a reserved word in JavaScript, so JSX uses className instead. When rendered, className is translated into the class attribute.

sections.heading: Comments in JSX
sections.content: Comments inside JSX are written as {/* comment */}.

sections.heading: JSX in React Components
sections.content: Components are independent, reusable bits of code, like JavaScript functions that return HTML. JSX works perfectly inside React components.

keyTakeaways: JSX = JavaScript XML, syntax extension to write HTML inside JS.
Use className instead of class.
All JSX elements must be properly closed.
Embed JS expressions using { }.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: React JSX Expressions

sections.heading: Expressions
sections.content: Insert any valid JavaScript expression inside JSX by wrapping it in curly braces { }. React evaluates the expression and renders the result in the DOM.

sections.heading: Variables
sections.content: Variables are valid expressions and can be inserted into JSX using { }.

sections.heading: Function Calls
sections.content: Function calls are valid expressions and can be inserted into JSX using { }.

sections.heading: Object Properties
sections.content: Access object properties within JSX using dot notation inside { }.

keyTakeaways: JSX expressions can be literals, variables, function calls, or object properties.
All must be wrapped inside single curly braces { }.

lessons.title: Lesson 1: React JSX Attributes

sections.heading: class = className
sections.content: Since class is a reserved JS keyword, JSX uses className. When rendered, className is translated back into class.

sections.heading: Expressions as Attributes
sections.content: You can use JavaScript expressions as attribute values. The value must NOT be wrapped in quotes when using an expression — quotes force JSX to treat it as a string literal instead of a JS expression.

sections.heading: camelCase Event Attributes
sections.content: Event attributes in JSX are written in camelCase, e.g. onClick, onChange.

sections.heading: Boolean Attributes
sections.content: If you pass no value for an attribute, JSX treats it as true. To pass false explicitly, you must specify it as an expression, e.g. disabled={false}.

sections.heading: The style Attribute
sections.content: The style attribute only accepts a JavaScript object with camelCased CSS property names (e.g. fontSize instead of font-size), not a CSS string like in HTML.

keyTakeaways: Use className, camelCase event handlers, and JS-object style attributes.
Expression attribute values are NOT quoted.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Styling React Using CSS

sections.heading: Inline Styling
sections.content: To style with the inline style attribute, the value must be a JavaScript object. Since JSX expressions use { } and JS objects also use { }, inline styling ends up written with double curly braces {{ }}.

sections.heading: camelCased Property Names
sections.content: CSS properties with hyphens (e.g. background-color) must be written in camelCase (backgroundColor) inside the style object.

sections.heading: JavaScript Object
sections.content: You can define a style object separately and reference it in the style attribute, instead of inlining it.

sections.heading: CSS Stylesheet
sections.content: You can write CSS in a separate .css file and import it into your component. Styles are only available to the component that imported the file.

sections.heading: CSS Modules
sections.content: CSS Modules (.module.css) scope styles locally to the importing component, avoiding name conflicts.

keyTakeaways: Three styling approaches: inline style object, CSS stylesheet import, CSS Modules.
Inline style uses {{ }} with camelCase keys.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: React CSS Modules

sections.heading: What are CSS Modules?
sections.content: CSS Modules are CSS files (.module.css) where class names are scoped locally by default, preventing class name collisions across components.

sections.heading: Creating a CSS Module
sections.content: Example: Button.module.css defines a .mybutton class.

sections.heading: Using a CSS Module
sections.content: Import the styles object and access classes via dot notation, e.g. styles.mybutton. The actual rendered class name is uniquely generated (e.g. _mybutton_q1obu_1).

sections.heading: Composing Classes
sections.content: CSS Modules support combining classes via the composes keyword, letting one class inherit another's styles.

sections.heading: Global Classes
sections.content: By default, CSS Module classes are scoped locally (prefixed with a unique hash). Use the :global(...) syntax to make a class available globally, unprefixed.

sections.heading: Combine Global and Local Classes
sections.content: A single CSS Module file can contain both globally-scoped and locally-scoped classes together.

keyTakeaways: CSS Modules auto-generate unique class names to avoid conflicts.
Use :global(...) to opt a class out of local scoping.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: React JSX If Statements

sections.heading: If statements are not allowed inside JSX
sections.content: React supports if statements, but NOT directly inside JSX markup. You must either place if logic outside the JSX, or use a ternary expression inline.

sections.heading: Option 1: if outside JSX
sections.content: Compute the value before the return statement, then reference the variable inside JSX.

sections.heading: Option 2: Ternary expression
sections.content: Use the ternary operator directly inside the JSX curly braces.

keyTakeaways: if/else cannot be written directly inside JSX braces.
Use either a precomputed variable, or a ternary operator inline.

lessons.title: Lesson 1: React Components

sections.heading: React Components
sections.content: Components are independent, reusable bits of code that work like JavaScript functions but return HTML/JSX. There are Function components and Class components — this course focuses on Function components combined with Hooks (the modern recommended approach).

sections.heading: Create Your First Component
sections.content: A component's name MUST start with an uppercase letter and return JSX.

sections.heading: Rendering a Component
sections.content: Use a component like an HTML tag: <Car />.
sections.code: createRoot(document.getElementById('root')).render(<Car />)

sections.heading: Components in Components
sections.content: Components can be referenced/nested inside other components, and can be rendered multiple times within a parent.

sections.heading: Components in Files
sections.content: Components are typically split into separate .jsx files (filename must start uppercase) and imported where needed, using export default / import.

keyTakeaways: Component names start with an uppercase letter.
Function components return JSX and can be nested/reused.
Split components into separate files using export default.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: React Props

sections.heading: React Props
sections.content: Props (properties) are arguments passed into components via HTML-like attributes, similar to function arguments in JavaScript.

sections.heading: Naming the props object
sections.content: The parameter name doesn't have to be 'props' — it can be called anything, e.g. myobj.

sections.heading: Multiple Properties & Data Types
sections.content: You can pass as many props as needed. Props can be any data type: strings (in quotes), or numbers/variables/objects/arrays (wrapped in curly braces { }).

sections.heading: Object and Array Props
sections.content: Object props are accessed via dot notation; array props via index notation.

sections.heading: Props are Read-only
sections.content: Props passed from parent to child are read-only. Attempting to modify a prop's value directly inside the child throws an error.

keyTakeaways: Props pass data from parent to child via attribute-like syntax.
Props are read-only and cannot be mutated by the child.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: React Destructuring Props

sections.heading: Destructuring Props
sections.content: Destructuring lets a component declare only the specific properties it needs from props, using curly braces.

sections.heading: Destructuring ...rest
sections.content: When you don't know how many properties you'll receive, use the ...rest operator to capture remaining properties not explicitly named into a single object.

sections.heading: Default Values
sections.content: With destructuring, you can assign default values for props; the default is used when no value is provided for that property.

keyTakeaways: Destructure props directly in the function signature: function Car({ brand, model }).
...rest captures unspecified props.
Default values: function Car({ color = "blue" }).

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Hooks and React useState

sections.heading: What is a Hook?
sections.content: Hooks are functions that let you 'hook into' React state and lifecycle features from functional components, without using classes. They give a direct API to props, state, context, refs, and lifecycle.

sections.heading: Hook Rules
sections.content: 1) Hooks can only be called inside React function components. 2) Hooks can only be called at the top level of a component. 3) Hooks cannot be conditional. Hooks do not work in class components.

sections.heading: Import & Initialize useState
sections.content: Import useState from 'react' and call it inside the component. useState accepts an initial state and returns an array of two values: the current state, and a function to update it.

sections.heading: Read State
sections.content: The current state value can be used anywhere inside the component's JSX.

sections.heading: Update State
sections.content: Use the updater function returned by useState to change state. Never mutate state directly (e.g. color = "blue" is NOT allowed).
sections.code: <button type="button" onClick={() => setColor("blue")}>Blue</button>

sections.heading: What Can State Hold?
sections.content: useState can track strings, numbers, booleans, arrays, objects, or any combination. You can use multiple useState calls for individual values, or a single useState holding an object.

sections.heading: Updating Objects and Arrays in State (Immutability)
sections.content: When state updates, the entire state value is overwritten — calling setCar({color: "blue"}) alone would wipe out the other object properties. Use the spread operator with a functional update to preserve previous state while changing only what's needed.

keyTakeaways: useState returns [value, setterFn]; never mutate state directly.
Hooks: top-level only, inside function components only, never conditional.
Use functional updates + spread operator ({ ...prev, key: value }) to update part of an object/array state immutably.
